name: Theyyam
html: From the word daivam, god. The ritual in which the koladhari, after hours of preparation, is believed to become the deity. Also called Kaliyattam, which is more often used for the festival.

name: Kolam
html: The form of the deity that a Theyyam takes, as in Theyyakkolam. People speak of someone “taking the kolam”, which means bearing the deity’s form.

name: Kaliyattam
html: The yearly festival of a shrine, grove or family house in North Malabar, held over one to several nights, in which Theyyams appear one after another. The word is also used loosely for Theyyam itself. Kaliyattams are community occasions that often draw very large crowds, so they are not the best first encounter. The season runs from about late October to May. See Kaliyattam 2027.

name: Perumkaliyattam
html: A very large Kaliyattam, held at long intervals, in which many Theyyams are held over several days. Sources give different intervals; Kerala Tourism says twelve years or more. See Kaliyattam 2027.

name: Ottakolam
html: A Theyyam that appears on its own, commonly explained as “a single kolam”, rather than together with other Theyyams. The word is often used for fire-linked forms such as Theechamundi and Vishnumoorthi, where the koladhari goes through a rite with embers. We found this meaning in a Wikipedia article and in general usage, not in a scholarly source, so please check it with a local guide.

name: Thottam and Vellattam
html: The first part of a Theyyam, held without full make-up or attire, with only a small red headdress. The koladhari sings or recites the story of the deity with the drummers.

name: Mudi
html: The sacred headdress. Placing it on the koladhari is described as the moment the deity enters. Night rituals may use a smaller mudi than the day ritual.

name: Mukhathezhuthu
html: Face painting, done by specialists in patterns that belong to each Theyyam, using natural colours.

name: Aniyara
html: The green room, a simple shelter near the grove where the koladhari is made up and dressed. A lamp is kept there, and in one account it is understood as the presence of God.

name: Purappadu
html: Roughly “coming forth”: the moment the fully dressed deity sets out from the green room towards the shrine ground. We found this word only in a few popular sources, so its use may vary.

name: Kalasam / kalasham
html: A word with more than one use. In some sources it is the closing stage, when the deity departs. In another it is a vessel with offerings placed on one side of the grove. In Wikipedia’s article, kalaasams are the eight sets of ritual footwork.

name: Kuri
html: A mark of blessing given by the deity, described in one account as dried turmeric and rice powder. Some deities use sacred ash instead.

name: Koladhari
html: The person who wears the kolam: the one through whom the deity is understood to appear.

name: Kavu
html: A sacred grove or small shrine, often the setting for a Theyyam.

name: Tharavad
html: An ancestral family home. Many Theyyams are kept by a tharavad as its family deity.

name: Madappura
html: A shrine of Muthappan. It has no idol or flagstaff and is open to people of all communities.

name: Banku
html: The Muslim call to prayer. Some Mappila Theyyams begin with it.
